acceptable.choice: Move report rendering out of the API request path into a background job queue on the Redis they already run (BullMQ), processed by a separate TypeScript/Node worker
acceptable.why: This fixes the real problem: CPU-bound rendering blocks the API's single Node event loop. It also reuses their existing stack, skills and infrastructure.

acceptable.choice: Run the worker as a separate Fly.io process group or app, built from the same repo and image, that scales on its own and has its own CPU allocation
acceptable.why: Separate machines mean month-end report load can't take CPU from the API. Fly process groups make this a small config change, not a new service to run.

acceptable.choice: Store the finished PDFs in object storage (S3, R2 or Tigris on Fly) and serve them through signed URLs, with job status shown by polling, an email, or a 'your report is ready' notification
acceptable.why: Each report is rendered once and then downloaded at no extra CPU cost. The API only hands out links, so it stays fast.

acceptable.choice: Pre-generate monthly reports in a batch as soon as the month's data is final, before customers come to download them
acceptable.why: Total work is about 3,000 × 0.4 s ≈ 20 CPU-minutes. Spreading that out ahead of time removes the month-end spike altogether and costs almost nothing.

acceptable.choice: As a short-term stopgap, move rendering into Node worker_threads (e.g. Piscina) inside the API process
acceptable.why: It unblocks the event loop quickly with little code change. It still shares the machine's CPU and memory with the API, though, so treat it as a bridge to a separate worker.

acceptable.choice: Serverless functions (AWS Lambda, or Vercel functions if the renderer fits their limits) triggered from the queue
acceptable.why: Bursty month-end load fits pay-per-use well. The trade-off is a second compute platform and cold-start or bundle-size limits, especially with headless Chromium.

acceptable.choice: Keep TypeScript for the report service
acceptable.why: The bottleneck is architecture, not language speed. Staying in TypeScript keeps one hiring profile, shared Prisma models and types, and quick shipping.

ruled_out.choice: Rewriting the report service in Go
ruled_out.why: Only one developer has some Go. A second language splits a four-person team's skills, the hiring pipeline and shared types/Prisma code, and it doesn't fix the cause (blocking in the request path). About 20 CPU-minutes a month doesn't justify it.

ruled_out.choice: Rewriting in Rust, or in Java/Kotlin on the JVM
ruled_out.why: Nobody on the team knows these or has run them in production. That's high operational and hiring cost for a workload too small to need the speed.

ruled_out.choice: Just scaling the API vertically or horizontally and leaving rendering inline
ruled_out.why: Rendering still blocks the event loop on whichever instance runs it. They'd be paying for capacity that sits idle most of the month, which works against a bill that should grow slower than revenue.

ruled_out.choice: Kubernetes, Kafka, or a full microservices split with its own repo, gRPC contracts and separate deploy pipeline
ruled_out.why: Far too much operational overhead for four developers on Fly/Vercel. Redis and a worker process already cover the need.

ruled_out.choice: Using cluster mode or adding more Node processes on the same machine as the whole fix
ruled_out.why: It helps a little, but renders still compete with API requests for the same CPU. It also doesn't isolate failures or memory spikes, especially with Chromium.

must_mention: Name the root cause: synchronous CPU-bound work blocks the Node.js event loop, so every other request waits. This is an architecture problem, not a language problem.
Do the maths: 3,000 × 400 ms ≈ 1,200 CPU-seconds ≈ 20 CPU-minutes spread over a few hours. That's a small load that one or two worker machines handle easily.
Make rendering asynchronous with a queue. They already have Redis for queues, so use it (e.g. BullMQ) instead of adding new infrastructure.
Run the workers on separate compute from the API so report load can't slow down other endpoints.
Store generated PDFs and serve them as files or signed URLs. Render each report once instead of on every download, and consider pre-generating before month end.

Advise against switching languages: stay in TypeScript for hiring, speed and shared code. Revisit only if measurement shows the renderer itself is the bottleneck, and even then try a faster TS/JS library before a rewrite.
Set worker concurrency, retries/idempotency and timeouts, and watch queue depth so a month-end backlog shows up and can be fixed by scaling workers.
red_flags: Recommending a rewrite in Go, Rust or a JVM language as the main fix, or implying the language is the cause
Ignoring the event-loop blocking explanation and only suggesting bigger or more API instances
Proposing new heavy infrastructure (Kubernetes, Kafka, RabbitMQ, a separate service mesh) when Redis queues already exist
Keeping rendering synchronous in the HTTP request while only tuning the code, leaving the API at risk at every month end
Running headless Chromium/Puppeteer inside the API process without noting its memory and CPU footprint
Recommending always-on large dedicated machines sized for the month-end peak without mentioning scale-to-zero or autoscaling of workers (bill concern)
Claiming specific performance gains from a language switch without any measurement
unknowns: Which rendering approach the prototype uses (headless Chromium/Puppeteer, react-pdf, pdfkit plus a chart library). This drives memory per job, worker sizing and whether serverless is practical.
Whether the 400 ms is really CPU in rendering, or includes database queries and chart data aggregation that could be optimised or cached separately
Whether report data is final at a known time, which decides whether pre-generating ahead of month end is possible
What download experience customers expect: instant download, or acceptable to wait seconds or minutes or get an email
Peak memory per render and the right worker concurrency on their Fly machine sizes
Whether month-end report queries also put noticeable load on the managed Postgres (may need a read replica or query tuning)
Whether reports must be rendered fresh on each download (e.g. live data, permissions) or can be cached and stored
